info.description:
ODE helps a developer build a SENERGY analytics operator: it profiles
the series behind a device, resolves a semantic intent to concrete
series, and runs code in the developer's own kernel — with an LLM
assistant whose reach over platform data is bounded by an exposure
tier (§3.2).

Every route except /health and /doc requires a bearer token carrying
the configured realm role. The platform API gateway validates the
token; ODE authorises on it (§3.1, D5). Routes appear only when
the capability behind them is configured, so a deployment without a
timescale-wrapper answers 404 on the profiler rather than 500.
info.title: Operator Development Environment

post.description:
Validates a declarative chart specification (§5.9), resolves every
series against the device type and the ontology, and stores it. No values
are read: this answers with the resolved units, the axis and the chart id,
and GET /charts/{id}/data is what reads the data behind it.

The resolution happens now rather than at first render so that a
`convert:` naming an unreachable characteristic is refused while the author
can still fix it — and because the device read it takes is the same
permission check the value read will need.

post.description:
Appends a developer confirmation, correction or rejection to the profiler's
override overlay (D21) from the exploration pane — an inferred unit, a
session boundary, a gap classification, an advised range (§5.10). It is the
same overlay the profiler view writes to and the same one every later
profile is resolved against, keyed by series rather than by profile, so a
confirmation survives recomputation and applies to a series that has never
been profiled at all.

A developer action only. §5.8 lists writing a ProfileOverride among the
operations with no LLM tool: a model that can confirm its own inferred unit
has confirmed nothing.

get.description:
Reads the series a specification names, on behalf of the caller, and
returns them with the profiler-derived annotations of §5.10: detected
sessions, gaps, advised exclusions and usable range, and counter-reset
markers. Every transform is evaluated by the platform (§5.3.1) — the
bucket, the counter differencing and the unit conversion are all fields of
POST /queries/v2, not arithmetic done here.

This is the only route in ODE that hands series values to a client, and it
hands them to the developer. The exposure tier bounds what an LLM sees; it
does not stand between a developer and their own data.

put.description:
Auto mode runs a `run_code` call without asking when its code is
recognised as an inspection of data already in the kernel — see
pkg/plaincode for what that means and, importantly, what it does not.
It is relief from repeated prompting, **not** a security boundary:
the boundary is unchanged and is the developer's own pod and token.
Anything unrecognised is still confirmed, and no other confirmed
tool is affected. No LLM tool exists for this.

put.description:
Sets the developer's own name for a conversation, in place of the
first few words of its opening message. An empty title clears the
name, and the next message titles the session again.

Its own sub-resource rather than a PUT of the whole session, so that
nothing changes a tier through a route that does not write §3.2's
audit trail.

put.description:
Changes the working context an existing conversation acts in: which
checkout its file tools write into, and which kernel its cells run in.
An empty workbench_id clears the assignment, which everything below
reads as "my only workbench".

The move leaves a note in the conversation. Every file read, file write
and cell run above it happened in the previous checkout, and a model
handed that history with no marker goes on believing the files it wrote
are still there.

Refused with 400 while a turn is running on the session: that turn is
acting in the workbench the move would take it away from.
put.summary: Move a session to another workbench

parameters.description: the workbench to act in; empty clears it
parameters.name: request

get.description:
Newest first. Statuses are refreshed from Ray for the runs that have
not finished, and only those — a listing of finished runs costs no
cluster calls. Resolved from the caller's own token: no route here takes

post.description:
Packages the developer's **committed** repository state with
`git archive`, uploads it to Ray, creates the MLflow run and tags it with
the commit SHA, then submits the job (§5.12, §5.11 item 7).

A working copy with uncommitted changes is refused with 409 and the
paths that made it dirty: the run records a commit SHA and is only
reproducible from it if the code that ran is that commit.

The job runs the operator's own training path: ODE hands it Operator
Lib's deployment config, and `MLOperator` opens the run, connects to
Ray, calls `train()` and registers the model. A launch with no
`input_topics` is refused with 400, because a run with no inputs reads
no history and fails inside `train()`.

parameters.description: the entrypoint, environment and run name
parameters.name: body

get.description:
The backend half of D6: each configured service is asked for its
X-Frame-Options and Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors, and the
verdict is cached with a TTL. `embeddable` is "yes", "no" or "unknown",
and **"unknown" is a real answer** — ODE is inside the cluster and the
browser is not, so a service ODE cannot reach may still frame perfectly.
The pane should still load a hidden iframe with a timeout and fall back
to a link-only card, which is the half only a browser can decide.
get.summary: Whether the Ray and MLflow UIs can be framed

parameters.description: re-probe rather than answering from the cache
parameters.name: refresh

get.description:
The record plus its status, refreshed from Ray unless the job has
already finished. Another developer's experiment answers 404 rather than
403: nothing here reveals that one exists.

§5.13's summary, the assistant's reading of it, the concrete next
adjustment it proposed, and the developer's decision on that proposal
if they have given one.

Recomputed rather than stored: the summary comes from MLflow, the
interpretation from the conversation the assistant wrote it in, and only
the decisions come from a table — the split §5.4.3 makes between a
recomputable artifact and a record of human judgement.

`proposal` carries an explicit `status: not_computed` where there is no
proposal: a run whose developer has not been connected since it finished
has not been interpreted yet, and that is a different fact from an
assistant that proposed nothing.

post.description:
§5.13's last sentence, recorded. Append-only and keyed by the
proposal's own fingerprint, so a rejected proposal stays rejected when the
same run is interpreted again, and a developer who changes their mind adds
a record rather than replacing one.

**Nothing here is binding (D28).** Accepting records agreement and
launches nothing; promoting a value into `evaluation.yaml` or the operator
config is a separate action the developer takes themselves, and §5.8 has no
tool for either. There is no LLM tool for this route: a model that could
accept its own proposal would be grading its own work.
post.summary: Accept, edit or reject a proposed next experiment

get.description:

summary and says raw logs never enter the model's context.

§5.13's compact structured summary: status, params, the latest value
of each metric, the run's tags, resource usage and the comparison against
the previous run of the same experiment. **Never logs** — those are a
route of their own, and no LLM tool reaches them.

post.description:
Asks Ray to stop it and reads the status back rather than assuming it:
Ray stops asynchronously, and a record claiming STOPPED while the job was
still winding down would disagree with the dashboard beside it. A job that
has already finished is answered with its record, not an error.

post.description:
Profiles every participating service, aligns the members onto one grid with
a single batched query, derives idle and active from each activity_pattern,
and proposes candidate rules with their exception windows (§5.5).

Values are read, so this is tier L1 for an LLM — but nothing that comes
back carries one: the document is contingency counts, ratios and bucket
durations.

Also available over the WebSocket as `relate`, which is the better route for
a wide window: the pass reads two passes per service plus the aligned read,
and the socket can cancel it.

get.description:
Turns an aspect node into candidate device sets (§5.5). The aspect
hierarchy is what solves candidate selection: the devices under "Kitchen"
yield the oven and the lights without the developer naming either.

Three kinds of set come back, in order of how much the grouping is worth
trusting: an existing platform device group, then one set per aspect node,
then the whole subtree. Every set names at least two devices, because a
single-device set has no conditional pattern in it.

Reads no values. The reads block says so, which is what makes the tier-L0
claim checkable from the answer.

It changes nothing. The working copy, the index and the remote are untouched,

get.description:
Whether this developer has connected a GitHub account, which account,
and whether the grant actually carries the scopes §5.11 item 1 needs.
Never the credential itself.

`?verify=true` additionally asks GitHub whether the stored credential
still works, and reports what it said: the status, GitHub's own message,
the scopes it reports for the token, and the token's *kind* — its public
prefix, which is what tells an OAuth app's non-expiring token from a
GitHub App's user token that expires in hours. Never any part of the
credential's value. Off by default because the pane polls this route and
a GitHub round trip per poll is not free.

The destructive answer of the three, so it requires `confirm: true` and

truncated and says so.

One working context each: a repository checkout and the kernel that
runs in it. Oldest first, so a picker does not reorder itself while
the developer is aiming at an entry.

Forgets it. The checkout stays on the PVC — it is the developer's work
and may hold uncommitted changes (§5.11 item 6) — and the kernel is
left running rather than killed, because something may still be in it.
Opening a workbench on the same repository again reuses the directory.

get.description:
One WebSocket carries everything that streams: profiler operations, the
chat exchange of §5.7, and kernel execution (§5.6). There is one
streaming mechanism rather than two, because an exchange can run for
minutes inside a single tool call and the connection has to survive it.

Not behind the usual middleware: a browser cannot set an Authorization
header on a handshake, so the token arrives in the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol
subprotocol or the query, and this handler enforces the realm role
itself. Everything else about §3.1 is unchanged.

parameters.description: bearer token, when the subprotocol cannot carry it
parameters.name: token

401.description: no token, or the required realm role is missing

allowed_providers.description:
AllowedProviders and AllowedModels narrow what may be used. Empty means "no
restriction beyond what the providers themselves declare", which is the
permissive default a fresh deployment wants.

global_cost_cap.description:
GlobalCostCap is the spend cap across every user. Meaningful only on the
global record; ignored on a per-user one, because a single user cannot own
the whole deployment's ceiling.

kernel_cpu_default.description:
Kernel and Ray caps are §3.3 fields ODE stores and does not enforce, and the
two have different reasons now that M4 exists.

The Ray cap waits for M7, as before. The kernel caps turned out not to be
ODE's to apply at all: a pod's resources are set by KubeSpawner at spawn
time, and the Hub API's spawn body selects a *profile* rather than carrying
arbitrary overrides. A per-user memory limit therefore lives in the
KubeSpawner profile itself, or in a Hub-side spawn hook — somewhere ODE
cannot reach from here.

They stay on the type because §3.3 lists them and an admin will look for
them, and DeclaredFields is what stops an administrator setting one and
assuming it binds.

max_concurrent_sessions.description: MaxConcurrentSessions caps live chat sessions per user.

max_tier.description:
MaxTier is the highest exposure tier this subject may raise a session to
(§3.3: "Maximum exposure tier permitted per user or globally"). Absent means
L2, the highest that exists.

max_workbenches.description:
MaxWorkbenches caps how many working contexts a developer may hold open.
Absent takes the deployment's own ceiling (repo_max_workbenches).

Unlike the kernel resource fields below, this one ODE can enforce, because
what it bounds is how many kernels ODE starts in a pod rather than how large
the pod is. The two belong together in an administrator's head: raising this
without raising the profile's memory is how a developer's training run gets
OOM-killed by their own second workbench.

period.description:
Period is the window a cap applies over, as a Go duration ("720h"). Empty
means the default.

soft_warn_fraction.description:
SoftWarnFraction is where a warning is raised, as a fraction of the hard cap
(0.8 = warn at four fifths). A warning changes nothing about whether the
request runs; it is surfaced so a developer is not cut off without notice.

token_cap.description:
TokenCap and CostCap are hard caps: a request that would exceed one is
refused. CostCap is in the pricing currency.

scaffold.description:
Scaffold defaults to true, which is why it is a pointer: an absent field and
an explicit false have to be told apart, and a created repository with no
scaffold is not what anyone asked for.

confirmed.description:
Confirmed is the developer's own form of the rule, required for a correction —
a narrowed statement, exceptions they added, exceptions they struck out.

entrypoint.description: Entrypoint is the command Ray runs. Empty takes the deployment's default.

env_vars.description:
EnvVars are extra environment variables for the job, validated at the service
boundary: bounded in count and size, and unable to override what ODE sets.

input_topics.description:
InputTopics are the operator's inputs. They decide what history the run reads,
so a launch without them is refused rather than run against nothing.

session_id.description:
SessionID ties the run to a chat session, so §5.13's summary can be injected
back into the conversation it came from.

export_id.description:
ExportID profiles an export instead of a device's service. Exclusive with
the two above.

edited.description: Edited is the developer's own form of the adjustment, required for an edit.

proposal_id.description:
ProposalID is what the developer was looking at. Required, and checked against
the proposal that currently stands: deciding on a stale one is answered with a
409 rather than recorded as agreement with something else.

function_ids.description:
The explicit id lists bypass the lexical matcher. They are how a caller that
has already read the ontology — an LLM in M3 — asks for exactly what it
means, and how a developer pins one half of a query.

rank.description:
Rank defaults to true when absent, which is why it is a pointer: §5.2 ranks
candidates by QuickProfile rather than returning them unordered. Sending
false asks for the ontology resolution alone, which costs no per-device
round trip.

title.description:
Title is the developer's own name for it. Optional: without one the label
falls back to the repository, and before there is one, to the id.

annotation_id.description:
AnnotationID is minted by ODE, not by the spec author: it is what a
confirmation refers back to, so it has to be unforgeable within a chart.

author.description:
Author is stamped by ODE. A derived annotation is profiler-authored and is
added at read time, so it cannot be forged in a spec.

confirmable.description:
Confirmable marks an annotation the developer may confirm, correct or reject
into the override overlay (§5.10). It requires FieldPath, because a
confirmation with nowhere to go is theatre.

series_index.description:
SeriesIndex is which series the annotation belongs to, or nil for the whole
chart. A confirmation needs it: the overlay is keyed by series reference.

source.description: Source is the free-text provenance of §5.9 ("profiler.sessions").

characteristic_id.description:
CharacteristicID is nil where none resolved. Never fabricated: a made-up id
would silently authorise a wrong server-side conversion (D29).

confirmable.description:
Confirmable says the developer's confirmation would add something: the unit
was inferred, is unknown, is in conflict, or travels in the message. Where
the ontology answered it outright there is nothing to confirm, which is
§5.10's own point — the ontology reduces how often confirmation is needed.

confirmed.description:
Confirmed and the two fields under it are the override overlay made visible.
ComputedUnit is what the resolver said before the developer spoke, so the
pane can show "W → kW, confirmed by …" rather than only the answer (§5.4.3).

from.description:
From records where the label came from: the specification's own y_axis, the
resolved series, or nothing that agreed.

mixed.description:
Mixed says the series do not share a unit. The chart still draws — comparing
a power series with a temperature is a legitimate thing to want to look at —
but the axis label would be a lie, so the pane says so instead.

note.description:
Note explains an unusual state — a conflict, a rejection, a unit that only
exists per message.

confirmable.description:
Confirmable is the closed set of paths, echoed for the same reason the
profiler route echoes it: the backend is authoritative and a client that has
drifted should be able to see it.

annotations_dropped.description:
AnnotationsDropped is how many bands the cap removed. Never silent: a chart
showing fifty of four hundred sessions looks like a chart of fifty.

group_time.description:
GroupTime is the chart-wide bucket; Aligned says whether every series shares
it.

confirmations.description:
Confirmations is the override overlay for this series, so the pane can show
what the developer has already decided next to what the detectors said.

non_numeric_dropped.description:
NonNumeric is how many returned values were not numbers, and NullRows how
many rows carried nothing for this variable. Both are reported rather than
dropped quietly: a line with half its points missing looks like a sparse
series, and the cause matters (D24's distinction again).

notes.description:
Notes carries anything the resolution had to say about this series — a
widened bucket, a refused conversion, a unit that needs confirming.

Notes carries anything the resolution had to say about this series — a
widened bucket, a refused conversion, a unit that needs confirming.

profile_id.description:
ProfileID names the profile the profiler-derived annotations come from
(§5.10). Optional: a chart of a series nobody has profiled still draws, it
just carries no detected sessions or gaps.

group_time.description:
GroupTime is the chart-wide aggregation bucket. Empty means "derive one that
fits the point cap", which is the normal case: a spec author knows the shape
they want to see, not how many points a browser should draw.

One bucket for the whole chart rather than one per series is §5.3.1 item 4:
alignment across series is a property of the request. A series may still
override it with resample:, and the response says when that has cost
alignment.

session_id.description:
SessionID ties a chart the model proposed to the conversation it was
proposed in, so the pane can list "the charts of this session". Empty for a
chart the developer built themselves.

window.description: Window is the range the chart covers. Absolute, and resolved at creation.

characteristic_id.description:
CharacteristicID is nil where none resolved. Never fabricated: a made-up id
would silently authorise a wrong server-side conversion (D29).

confirmable.description:
Confirmable says the developer's confirmation would add something: the unit
was inferred, is unknown, is in conflict, or travels in the message. Where
the ontology answered it outright there is nothing to confirm, which is
§5.10's own point — the ontology reduces how often confirmation is needed.

confirmed.description:
Confirmed and the two fields under it are the override overlay made visible.
ComputedUnit is what the resolver said before the developer spoke, so the
pane can show "W → kW, confirmed by …" rather than only the answer (§5.4.3).

note.description:
Note explains an unusual state — a conflict, a rejection, a unit that only
exists per message.

auto_run.description:
AutoRun is the developer's standing answer to a `run_code` confirmation whose
code pkg/plaincode recognises: run it rather than asking again.

Per session, not per developer, because the exposure a conversation is
working at is already a per-session decision and this belongs beside it. Off
unless turned on, and turning it on is a developer action with no tool behind
it — `set_auto_run` is in the denied set for the same reason
`set_exposure_tier` is, so a model cannot widen what it is allowed to do
without being asked.

It is a convenience and not a boundary. See pkg/plaincode.

exposure_tier.description: Tier is the exposure tier (§3.2). Default L0.

message_count.description: MessageCount lets a listing show session size without loading every message.

selection.description:
Selection is the data selection the developer has confirmed, if any (§5.2's
last step). Stored on the session because §5.10 says confirmations persist as
session overrides.

user_sub.description:
UserSub owns the session. Every read checks it: a session id in a URL must
not be enough to read someone else's conversation.

workbench_id.description:
WorkbenchID is the working context this conversation acts in: which checkout
write_file writes into, and which kernel run_code runs in. Two sessions may
name the same one — talking about one operator from two angles — or different
ones, which is a developer working on two operators at once.

Empty is a session written before workbenches existed, or one whose workbench
has since been closed. Both resolve to the developer's only workbench when
they have one, so no conversation loses its code context.

expires_in_seconds.description:
ExpiresIn is how long the job's token is good for, as the issuer reported it.
Zero when unknown, which is the honest answer for a session token: ODE does
not validate tokens (§3.1 step 2) and does not read their expiry.

expires_with_session.description:
ExpiresWithSession is the limitation, stated. True means a run outliving the
developer's session will lose its platform access partway through.

note.description:
Note is the sentence a pane or a model shows. Written here rather than at
each call site so both say the same thing.

source.description:
Source is "exchanged" — a token minted for this job through the Keycloak
token exchange — or "session", the caller's own.

goal.description:
Goal is "minimise" or "maximise", and GoalStated says whether the file said so
or whether it was inferred from the metric's name. The pair is here for the
reason MetricDelta carries LowerIsBetter: a verdict whose rule is invisible
reads as a judgement, and "assuming lower rmse is better" is a sentence a
model should be able to say.

met.description: Met is true, false, or a not_computed object naming the reason.

source.description:
Source names where the criterion came from — the developer's file at a commit,
or the run's own tags — so nobody reads the verdict as ODE's own opinion.

threshold.description:
Threshold is a pointer for the reason Value is: `omitempty` on a float64 would
hide a threshold of exactly zero, which is what §5.11 item 3's scaffold ships,
while a plain float64 put `"threshold": 0` into every criterion that has none —
a number the developer never wrote, in the document a model reads.

value.description:
Value is what the run logged for the metric. A pointer because a metric of
exactly zero is a real reading and `omitempty` on a float64 would hide it,
while a metric the run never logged has to be visibly absent.

reason.description:
Reason is the header that decided it, or why nothing did. Carried because
"no" without the header is not actionable by whoever has to change it.

status.description:
Status is the HTTP status the probe got. Zero when the service could not be
reached at all.

cached.description: Cached says this answer came from the TTL cache rather than a fresh probe.

experiment_id.description:
ID is ODE's own identifier, the one that appears in URLs. Separate from
SubmissionID because the two have different owners: a Ray cluster may be
replaced, and a developer's own list of what they ran should survive that.

message.description: Message is Ray's own, for a job that failed. Never a log.

mlflow_run_id.description: RunID and MLflowExperimentID are the run ODE created before submitting.

package_reused.description:
PackageReused says the archive was already on the cluster and was not
uploaded again. Two launches from the same commit produce the same bytes.

package_uri.description:
PackageURI is the gcs:// URI of the working directory Ray unpacks, and
PackageBytes its size — reported because it is the one number a developer can
act on when a launch is refused for exceeding the cap.

repository.description: Repository is owner/name, and CommitSHA the state the package was built from.

scoped_credential.description:
ScopedCredential says whether the job carries a token of its own (§3.1 item
6) or the caller's session token. False is a supported deployment and a
stated limitation, not a fault — see Credential.

session_id.description:
SessionID is the chat session this was launched from, when it was. One of the
four metadata keys §5.12 names.

submission_id.description:
SubmissionID is what Ray was asked to call the job. ODE mints it rather than
letting Ray, so a resubmission of the same request cannot silently become two
jobs: Ray rejects a duplicate submission id.

workbench_id.description:
WorkbenchID is the working context the package came from: which checkout, and
which kernel packaged it. Kept so an interpretation months later reads this
run's own evaluation.yaml rather than whichever workbench happens to be the
developer's only one by then.

filterType.description: FilterType is "DeviceId" or "OperatorId"; FilterValue the id it matches.

experiment_id.description:
ID is ODE's own identifier, the one that appears in URLs. Separate from
SubmissionID because the two have different owners: a Ray cluster may be
replaced, and a developer's own list of what they ran should survive that.

message.description: Message is Ray's own, for a job that failed. Never a log.

mlflow_run_id.description: RunID and MLflowExperimentID are the run ODE created before submitting.

mlflow_tracking_uri.description:
TrackingURI is what the job was told MLflow is, so a developer can open the
run without knowing ODE's configuration.

package_reused.description:
PackageReused says the archive was already on the cluster and was not
uploaded again. Two launches from the same commit produce the same bytes.

package_uri.description:
PackageURI is the gcs:// URI of the working directory Ray unpacks, and
PackageBytes its size — reported because it is the one number a developer can
act on when a launch is refused for exceeding the cap.

repository.description: Repository is owner/name, and CommitSHA the state the package was built from.

scoped_credential.description:
ScopedCredential says whether the job carries a token of its own (§3.1 item
6) or the caller's session token. False is a supported deployment and a
stated limitation, not a fault — see Credential.

session_id.description:
SessionID is the chat session this was launched from, when it was. One of the
four metadata keys §5.12 names.

submission_id.description:
SubmissionID is what Ray was asked to call the job. ODE mints it rather than
letting Ray, so a resubmission of the same request cannot silently become two
jobs: Ray rejects a duplicate submission id.

warnings.description:
Warnings are things that did not stop the launch but that the developer
should read — a token exchange that answered with a shorter lifetime than the
deployment asked for, for instance.

workbench_id.description:
WorkbenchID is the working context the package came from: which checkout, and
which kernel packaged it. Kept so an interpretation months later reads this
run's own evaluation.yaml rather than whichever workbench happens to be the
developer's only one by then.

direction.description:
Direction is §5.13's "better|worse", and LowerIsBetter is how it was decided.

The two are separate on purpose. Whether a smaller number is an improvement
is a property of the metric, and without the developer's evaluation criteria
ODE can only go by the name — loss, error, mae, rmse and mape count down,
everything else counts up. Carrying the rule beside the verdict means a model
reading this can say "assuming lower rmse is better" instead of asserting an
improvement it inferred from a naming convention.

peak_memory_source.description:
PeakMemorySource is empty when the job reported no memory metric, which is
the normal case. Present rather than a silent zero, for D24's reason: a zero
read as "used no memory" would be a fabricated finding.

comparison_to_previous.description:
ComparisonToPrevious is this run against the previous finished run of the
same MLflow experiment — which, per D17, is the same developer on the same
repository. Empty when there is no previous run, and that is worth reading as
"first run" rather than "no change".

evaluation_criteria.description:
EvaluationCriteria is §5.13's block: the developer's own criterion, from their
`evaluation.yaml` at the run's commit, graded against what the run logged.

**Always present, never absent.** A run with no criteria file, a file ODE
could not read, a summary built before the developer was back — each is a
criterion whose `met` is an explicit non-result with a reason, not a criterion
that is missing. Absence would be read as "there was nothing to meet"; D24 is
the same rule the profiler applies to a detector's field, and it applies here
for the same reason.

finished.description:
Finished says the run is in a state it will not leave, so a model can tell a
final metric from a snapshot of one still moving.

note.description:
Note carries what a reader would otherwise have to infer: that a run is still
going, that there was nothing to compare against, that Ray and MLflow
disagreed.

previous_run_id.description:
PreviousRunID names what the comparison is against, so a claim about an
improvement can be checked.

secondary_criteria.description:
SecondaryCriteria are the other metrics the file asks to watch. Beyond §5.13's
literal shape, and here because §5.11 item 3's scaffold has a
`secondary_metrics` key and silently dropping what a developer wrote there
would make the summary a partial reading of their own file.

status.description:
Status is the run's, which is Ray's job status reconciled with MLflow's own.
Where they disagree Ray wins for a job still running and MLflow for a
finished one — see reconcile.

decision.description:
Decision is the developer's answer, if they have given one. The latest record
in the log, merged at read time — never written into this document, for the
reason §5.4.3 gives about the override overlay: the computed artifact and the
human judgement stay separable, and "the assistant proposed X and the developer
rejected it" is the finding.

decisions.description:
Decisions is the whole log for this proposal, oldest first. A developer who
changed their mind added a record rather than replacing one.

interpretation.description:
Interpretation is what the assistant said, in full. Empty until the turn has
run, which is what InterpretedAt being zero means.

proposal.description: Proposal is the concrete next adjustment, or an explicit non-result.

summary.description: Summary is §5.13's structured document, as it was injected.

summary_at.description:
SummaryAt is when it was built, which is when the run became terminal — not
when the developer came back to it.

proposal_id.description:
ID is a fingerprint of what was proposed, for this experiment.

Keyed on the text rather than on the interpretation it appeared in, which is
what makes a decision survive a recomputation — the same choice
relations.RuleDecision makes for the same reason. Re-interpreting a run that
produces the same proposal produces the same id, so a rejection still stands;
a materially different proposal is a different id and is asked about again.

status.description:
Status is empty when there is a proposal, and "not_computed" with a reason
when the assistant named none.

text.description: Text is the adjustment, in the assistant's own words.

binding.description:
Binding is always false, and is serialised rather than omitted so that a
reader meets D28 rather than having to know it: accepting a proposal records
agreement and changes nothing. Promoting a value into evaluation.yaml or the
operator config is a separate act the developer performs themselves, and §5.8
has no tool for it either.

edited.description:
Edited is the developer's own form of the adjustment. Required for an edit and
empty otherwise, because an edit whose content was not recorded is a rejection
with extra steps.

proposal_id.description: ProposalID is what the decision is keyed by — see Proposal.ID.

proposed.description:
Proposed is the assistant's own wording, copied in rather than referenced.
The record has to stay readable after the interpretation it came from has been
evicted from memory, and "what was actually proposed" is half the finding.

run_id.description:
RunID records which MLflow run the proposal was about, so the log is readable
after ODE's own record of the experiment is gone.

children.description: Children is set on a directory when the listing was recursive.

elided.description:
Elided says this directory holds more entries than the walk was allowed to
report. Reported rather than silently cut, for the reason D26 gives about
projections: a truncated tree read as a complete one is the failure.

path.description: Path is relative to the workspace root, with forward slashes.

busy.description:
Busy is true while an execution ODE started is still running in this kernel.
One workbench's own kernel only: a busy workbench says nothing about another.

directory.description:
Directory is where this kernel actually runs, workspace-relative and empty
for the root. It is the workbench's checkout, so `open("notes.txt")` in a
cell lands next to the operator's code.

kernel_count.description:
KernelCount is how many kernels ODE is holding in this pod. Reported because
each one is a Python process in a pod with one memory limit, and a developer
wondering why their run was killed should be able to see it.

profile.description: Profile is the KubeSpawner profile ODE spawns with, empty for the default.

workbench.description:
Workbench is which working context this kernel belongs to, empty for the
default one.

workspace.description:
Workspace is the persistent working directory tree, the root of everything on
the PVC.

workspace_ready.description: WorkspaceReady says the directory exists on the PVC.

counted.description:
Counted is false for a column the probe could not ask about — an unreadable
column name, an unknown type. Reason says which.

rows.description:
Rows is how many rows of the counted window carry a value here. Zero beside
a non-zero ExportFill.Rows is the null-column case, and Empty says so
without the reader having to compare the two.

buckets_with_rows.description:
BucketsWithRows is how many buckets of the counted window contained at least
one row, null columns included.

This is what distinguishes "nothing was written" from "everything written is
null", and it is readable off the response because the server groups by the
bucket: a bucket appears in the answer only where a row falls in it, and it
appears with a count of zero for a column that is null in every row of it.
Without this, an export whose value paths all miss would report as empty —
which is the one wrong answer here, because it sends a developer to look at
the topic rather than at the paths.

reason.description:
Reason says why, in the words a developer needs, for every state including
the good one. Never empty.

rows.description:
Rows is how many rows of the counted window carry a value in at least one
column, taken from the column that carries the most.

It is not the row count, and the difference is the whole point of this
answer: an export whose every column is null has rows and reports 0 here.
BucketsWithRows is what says rows exist at all.

span.description:
Span is the first and last bucket that carried a row, at bucket resolution.
It is what stands in for an availability window: a profile over an export is
bounded by this, and its coarseness is the reason Bucket is reported beside
it.

usage.description:
Usage is /usage/exports, which is metadata and reads nothing. Absent is an
ordinary answer: the usage table is filled per timescale table by a
collector, so a young export has no row in it.

window.description: Window is the range the counts were taken over.

series_ref.description:
SeriesRef is what an override is keyed by. ProfileID records which profile
the developer was looking at, and DetectorVersion which detectors produced
it, so a confirmation made against an old detector can be reviewed rather
than silently carried forward — but neither is used for lookup, because a
recomputation changes both and the confirmation has to survive it.

limit_reduced.description:
LimitReduced says the first attempt was refused by the gateway and the read
was retried with fewer rows. A short raw window then has a third possible
cause — neither retention nor the developer's setting — and guessing between
them is exactly what D24 exists to prevent.

row_limit.description:
RowLimit is the row cap the read was actually made with.

It is not the configured figure: the raw read is one wide row per message
carrying one value per variable, so the response costs rows times variables,
and the cap that bounds it is divided by the variables being read. Recording
the applied number is what makes a short raw window legible — a developer
looking at four days where they configured fourteen should be able to see why
without reading the source.

omitempty for one reason worth knowing: a profile captured before this field
existed still satisfies the shape. Any profile this build computes carries it.

truncated.description:
Truncated says the point limit cut the window short, in which case From
is the oldest point actually read rather than the one requested. Without
this the gap detector would report a gap that is only a missing read.

aggregated_buckets.description: AggregatedBuckets is how many buckets the aggregated pass returned.

diagnosis.description:
Diagnosis names the cause when there is one to name, in the terms a reader
can act on. Empty when both passes returned data.

raw_available.description:
RawAvailable is what /data-availability says: false means the platform holds
only aggregated buckets for this service, so there is no unbucketed data to
read and every structural detector is dead on arrival. Retention causes this,
and it is the first thing to check on an empty profile.

A Value rather than a bool because the endpoint can fail, and a bool cannot
tell "the platform says there is no raw window" from "the platform could not
be asked". That is precisely the distinction D24 exists to keep: read as a
false, an unanswered probe would send a reader looking for retention that is
not the cause. When it is not computed the reason is read_failed and the
detail is the platform's own error.

raw_rows.description: RawRows is how many rows the raw pass returned for the whole service.

values_present.description:
ValuesPresent is how many of those rows carried a value for *this* variable,
and NullRows how many did not. A service can report while one of its channels
stays silent, which looks identical to a dead read from inside a single
variable's profile.

implied_scale.description:
ImpliedScale is the factor that best maps the other series onto this one.
For a counter against a rate it is the unit ratio, so a value near 3600
says watt-hours against watts and a value near 1 says watt-seconds — which
is how a unit error shows up as a number rather than as a failed check.

cache_key.description:
CacheKey is carried in the body as well as being the store's key, so a
profile handed around outside the store can still be checked for staleness.

read_summary.description:
ReadSummary says what the two passes actually returned for this variable.

It exists because a profile full of not_computed is otherwise a puzzle: the
fields report their own reason honestly, but "no sampling interval" is the
symptom, and the cause — nothing came back, or rows came back with no value
in this column, or there is no raw data to read at all — lives one level
down where nobody can see it. This is the one block that is always populated.

characteristic_id.description:
CharacteristicID is canonical and authoritative; Unit is derived from it
and advisory (D29). It is a pointer because null is a legitimate value
where the unit was inferred, and fabricating an id here would silently
enable a wrong server-side conversion.

depth.description: Depth is 0 for the requested node.

advisory.description:
Advisory states the boundary in the document itself, so a model reading a
projection of this cannot mistake a candidate for a configured rule.

decision.description:
Decision is the developer's, re-injected from the append-only log when the
same rule is computed again. Nil means nobody has decided yet.

exceptions.description:
Exceptions are the conditions under which the rule does not hold — the
"except at certain times of day" of the motivating case. Empty means it held
in every condition examined, which is a finding rather than a missing field.

rule_id.description:
RuleID is a fingerprint of what the rule *says* — the two members, their
states, and the direction. It deliberately excludes the window, the grid and
the detector version, so a decision made today still applies to the same rule
recomputed next month over a different window (D21).

samples.description:
Samples is how many buckets the antecedent held in, and Violations how many
of those the consequent failed in. Violations is the count of the anomaly the
rule defines, which is the figure a developer judges it by.

statement.description:
Statement is the rule in words, and Anomaly is its violation in words. Both
are generated rather than templated at the call site, because they are what
appears beside the confirm button and the two have to agree.

strength.description:
Strength is this detector's own certainty, and it is ordinal because D23
forbids inventing a probability for it. It is not the confidence above: that
is P(consequent | antecedent), a statistic; this is how much weight the
detector puts on the finding given how much evidence there is.

support.description:
Support, Confidence and Lift are the association statistics §5.5 names. They
are ratios with definitions, unlike Strength below.

aspect_path.description:
AspectPath is root-first, so a reader can see where "Kitchen" sits without
fetching the tree.

devices.description:
Devices is how many distinct devices the members span. A set of one device is
not a multi-device pattern, which is why it is never proposed.

graph_id.description:
The graph a set came from, and the node its members meet at. Empty for a set the
aspect hierarchy or a device group proposed.

rationale.description:
Rationale says why these devices are together, in the terms the developer can
judge — "both report under the aspect Kitchen" rather than a score.

set_id.description:
SetID is a fingerprint of the origin and the members, so the same proposal
made twice carries the same id and a relation can name where its members came
from.

truncated.description:
Truncated says the member cap applied, and Notes says what was left out. A
silent truncation reads as completeness.

bucket.description: Bucket is the condition in a form a person reads: "06:00-12:00", "weekend".

active_active.description: The counts, named by the state of A then of B.

active_rate_a.description:
ActiveRateA and ActiveRateB are the marginals, and they are what a lift is
measured against.

observed.description:
Observed is the sum of the four, which is the number of buckets in which both
members had a reading.

drop.description:
Drop is how far below the rule's overall confidence this condition fell. It
is the reason the exception was raised and belongs beside it.

from_hour.description:
FromHour and ToHour bound an hour-of-day exception, half-open, in UTC — the
machine-readable form of Bucket. Both are zero for a weekday/weekend
exception, which Dimension already identifies.

depth.description:
Depth is how many edges separate this member from the graph's sink. It is what
makes "these two are at the same level" and "one contains the other" visible
without walking the topology again.

role.description: Role is sibling, upstream or downstream.

via.description:
Via is the node this member's flow reaches, and ViaName its label. For a
downstream member of a flow set it is the node they all feed, which that member
measures.

weight.description:
Weight is the edge weight out of this device toward Via.

It is an *output split*, not a contribution share, and the difference matters
when reading one: models.Graph.Valid requires the outgoing weights of each node
to sum to 100, so a device feeding exactly one node always carries 100 and says
nothing. Below that means the device's flow is allocated across several
downstream nodes — one meter split across two business units, say — and only then
is the figure a fact about this edge rather than about the node having one.

Zero where the member has no outgoing edge at all: the sink end of a flow set.

profile_id.description:
ProfileID is the SeriesProfile the state series was derived from, so a
reader can go and look at the threshold rather than take it on trust.

state.description:
State is how idle and active were decided for this member, including whether
the threshold was the detector's or the developer's.

unit.description:
Unit and Kind are carried because a rule about a cumulative counter is a rule
about its rate, and that distinction has to be visible where the rule is read.

a.description:
A and B index RelationProfile.Members. Indices rather than references because
the same series may legitimately appear twice under different labels, and a
reference would then be ambiguous.

conditions.description: Conditions is Overall split by the conditioning dimensions.

overall.description:
Overall is the joint distribution over every bucket both members were
observed in.

candidate_devices.description:
CandidateDevices is every readable device the aspect resolved to, whether or
not it made it into a set. It is what makes "only one device here" visible.

include_descendants.description:
IncludeDescendants is echoed because it changes the answer materially and the
caller may have relied on a default.

reads.description:
Reads is structurally value-free: this operation is tier L0 (§5.8) and reads
the ontology, the device list and the device groups. A non-zero Values here
would mean the tier claim had been broken.

subtree.description: Subtree is the aspect nodes that were considered, root-first.

devices.description:
Devices is the metadata reads: one per service a pass profiles, and one per
graph neighbour a proposal resolves from outside the requested aspect. Counted
separately from Values because a device read is metadata and does not touch the
tier — but counted, because a proposal that quietly made twelve of them would
otherwise look free.

values.description:
Values totals the value-reading passes, so a caller comparing this against a
QuickProfile's zero has one number to compare.

buckets.description:
Buckets is the length of the aligned grid, and Observed how many buckets had
a reading from every usable member. A rule's support is a share of Observed,
not of Buckets, and stating both is what keeps that legible.

cache_key.description:
CacheKey is the relation id, for the same reason the profiler's is: a caller
holding a relation can check it for staleness without a second index.

candidate_set_id.description:
CandidateSetID names the proposal this pass came from, when it came from one.
It is how a confirmed rule can be traced back to the aspect that suggested
the devices.

tier.description:
Tier is the lowest exposure tier at which this document may be shown to a
model. It is L1 throughout — contingency counts and durations are aggregates,
and no value of any series appears here.

computed.description:
Computed is the rule as the detector stated it — the statement and the three
figures. Copied into the record rather than referenced, because the record has
to stay readable after the relation profile it came from has been evicted, and
because "the detector said 0.91 and the developer confirmed it" is the finding.

confirmed.description:
Confirmed is the developer's own form of the rule, for a correction: a narrowed
statement, exceptions they added, exceptions they struck out. Nil for a plain
confirm or reject.

relation_id.description:
RelationID and DetectorVersion record what the developer was looking at, so a
decision made against an older detector can be reviewed rather than carried
forward unexamined. Neither is used for lookup.

exception_drop.description:
ExceptionDrop is how far a conditioned confidence must fall below the rule's
overall confidence before that condition is reported as an exception.

hour_buckets.description:
HourBuckets is how many equal parts the day is split into for conditioning.
Four is deliberately coarse: twenty-four buckets over a month leave too few
samples each to distinguish an exception from noise.

min_confidence.description:
MinConfidence is P(consequent | antecedent): how reliably the pattern holds
where the antecedent is true.

min_lift.description:
MinLift is how much more often the pair co-occurs than independent base rates
predict. Confidence alone promotes a consequent that is simply always true —
a light left on all year confirms every rule about it at confidence 1.0.

min_samples.description: MinSamples is the fewest antecedent-true buckets a rule may be built from.

min_support.description:
MinSupport is the share of observed buckets a pattern must cover. It is what
stops a rule resting on four coincidences in a year.

characteristic_id.description: CharacteristicID is canonical and never fabricated (§5.4.11).

from_aspect.description:
FromAspect says the member came from the requested aspect rather than being
reached through a graph. A graph legitimately crosses out of the aspect — a site
meter is not in the kitchen — so a reader comparing a set against the aspect they
asked about needs to know which members are which.

graph.description:
Graph is where this member sits in the topology that proposed it, and is nil for
a member the aspect hierarchy proposed. It changes how a rule about the member
should be read: a sibling and a sub-meter are different relationships, and the
weight says what share of the flow this device accounts for.

label.description:
Label is what a rule statement will call this member. Built from the device
name and the variable's last path segment, because "the oven's power" reads and
"urn:infai:ses:device:4711|…|value.power" does not.

active_buckets.description:
ActiveBuckets, IdleBuckets and UnknownBuckets are the state series as three
numbers, which is what makes a lift figure checkable by hand.

observed_buckets.description:
ObservedBuckets is how many aligned buckets carried a value for this member, and
it is populated whether or not a state series could be derived.

It is the one number that separates the two ways a member fails, and without it
they look identical: an unusable member reports 0 active, 0 idle and every bucket
unknown either because the read came back empty or because it came back full and
no idle/active split could be found in it. Those have different causes and
different fixes, and "1 aligned read" says the read happened, not what it
returned.

reason.description:
Reason is a pointer because omitempty does not apply to a struct: as a value it
would put an empty reason object beside every *usable* member, which is exactly
the "there is a reason and it is blank" reading D24 exists to prevent. Absent
means there is nothing to explain, and Usable is what says so.

threshold.description:
Threshold is the value that separates idle from active, in the member's own
unit. Meaningless for a categorical member, which reports method "distinct".

threshold_source.description:
ThresholdSource is `detector` or `confirmed`. §5.10's whole argument rests on
the second being visible: a rule computed against a threshold the developer
corrected is a different claim from one computed against a guess.

usable.description:
Usable is false when no state series could be derived. The reason says why,
and the member then takes part in no rule rather than contributing a series
of silently-idle buckets.

redirect_uri.description:
RedirectURI is where GitHub will send the browser. Reported because it has to
match the OAuth app's registered callback exactly, and a mismatch is the most
common setup failure — naming it makes the error message actionable.

scopes.description:
Scopes is what ODE is asking for, reported so the SPA can say what the
consent screen will show.

kind.description:
Kind is "modified", "added", "deleted", "renamed", "copied", "untracked",
"unmerged" or "typechange" — git's XY codes, named.

renamed_from.description: RenamedFrom is the old path of a rename or a copy.

staged.description:
Staged and Unstaged are the two halves of git's XY, so the pane can show
what a commit would include. A file can be both.

branch.description:
Branch is where it landed, which for a first commit is the branch ODE put
HEAD on rather than one that existed before.

files.description:
Files is how many paths the commit touched, from git's own summary rather
than from what ODE staged — the two differ when a file was already staged.

committed.description:
Committed is always false, and is reported for the reason WriteResult's is:
it is the property that matters, and a caller that assumed otherwise would
tell the developer their work is saved.

files.description: Files is how many changed files the draft was written from.

message.description: Message is the draft: a subject line, a blank line, and a short body.

truncated.description:
Truncated says the diff did not fit the budget and was cut. Reported because
it changes how much a developer should trust the body.

language.description:
Language is a hint for the editor, derived from the extension. The backend
does it so the pane and `write_file` agree on what a `.py` is.

excluded.description:
Excluded names what the walk did not enter. `.git` and nothing else: a
developer may edit every file of their repository, but the object database is
not a file they edit — and listing it would bury the tree.

root.description: Root is the checkout, relative to the workspace.

missing_scopes.description:
MissingScopes names what the grant lacks of what §5.11 item 1 asks for. Empty
is the normal case; a non-empty list is reported to the developer up front
rather than discovered when a push is rejected.

operator_lib_ref.description:
OperatorLibRef is the Operator Lib the scaffold pinned, per D15: latest at
scaffold time, recorded so an upgrade is a visible decision later. Empty for
a repository ODE did not scaffold.

path.description:
Path is where the checkout is, relative to the workspace root — so
`{workspace}/{path}` on the PVC. Derived from the repository name and stable,
which is the "stable path" of §5.6.

workbench_id.description:
WorkbenchID is the working context this link belongs to. Carried on the link
as well as on the workbench because every operation below takes a link and
then has to say which kernel to run in, and threading it separately through
twenty call sites is how one of them ends up running in the wrong checkout.

head_sha.description:
HeadSHA is what the remote now has, so the experiment tag of §5.11 item 7
can be taken from a state that is actually pushed.

can_push.description:
Permissions.Push is why this field exists: a repository the developer can
only read is offered, but selecting it will fail on push, and saying so in
the list is cheaper than saying so afterwards.

hint.description:
Hint says what to do next, which after a scaffold is always the same thing:
read it, then commit it.

operator_lib_ref.description:
OperatorLibRef is the pin the developer now has, repeated here because it is
the one part of a scaffold that is a decision rather than a file.

complete.description:
Complete is Missing being empty — carried so the SPA does not have to know
that rule.

ahead.description:
Ahead and Behind are commits, relative to the upstream branch. Both non-zero
is Diverged, which is the case that needs a human.

cloned.description:
Cloned is false when the PVC has no checkout, which happens on a fresh PVC
and after a developer deletes the directory themselves.

detached.description:
Detached is a checkout not on a branch — nothing ODE does produces one, but a
developer with a terminal can, and committing there silently would lose work.

fetched.description:
Fetched says whether this status included a fetch. A status without one
reports the divergence ODE last knew about, and saying which it is prevents
reading a stale zero as "up to date".

remote.description:
Remote is the origin URL as the checkout has it, so a directory pointing at
a different repository than the link says is visible rather than silently
committed into.

remote_mismatch.description: RemoteMismatch is that case, made explicit.

scaffold.description:
Scaffold reports which of the compliance files of §5.11 item 3 are present.
A repository the developer brought themselves is usually missing some, and
this is what the pane offers to scaffold from.

unborn.description:
Unborn is a clone of an empty repository: a branch with no commits yet. It is
the normal state of a repository ODE has just created.

workspace.description:
Workspace and AbsolutePath say where the checkout is, because "it is on the
PVC" is not something a developer can act on.

last_used_at.description:
LastUsedAt orders the list and is what a picker shows first. Not a liveness
signal: whether a kernel is actually running is the kernel surface's answer.

link.description: Link is the repository this workbench works on. Zero until one is selected.

title.description:
Title is the developer's own name for it. Empty falls back to the repository
and, before there is one, to the id — see Label.

committed.description:
Committed is always false and is reported anyway, because it is the property
that matters: writing a file changes the working copy and nothing else
(§5.11 item 5). The `write_file` tool returns this to the model for the same
reason — so it does not tell the developer their change is pushed.

repository.description:
Repository is which working copy it landed in. Carried because a caller that
is not looking at the pane — the `write_file` tool — may have been told about
a different repository earlier in the same session.

name.description:
Name is the platform's display name where it has one (devices.DisplayName),
because this list exists to be read rather than joined on.

series.description:
Series is how many resolved series this device contributes, which is what
makes a device with forty matching paths distinguishable from one with a
single relevant column.

device_type_name.description:
DeviceTypeName is empty when no listed device carries this type; see
Selectable.DeviceTypeName.

proposed_at.description: ProposedAt is stamped by ODE rather than taken from the model.
